title: Medical device rep
tagline: Learn to sell medical devices to clinics and hospitals through value-based evidence and committee consensus.
setting: Conversations happen in clinic offices, hospital conference rooms, and virtual meetings where buying committees evaluate clinical and economic evidence.

scenarios.label: Virtual first meeting
scenarios.desc: A 30-minute video call with a clinical champion who screens vendors for the value analysis committee.
scenarios.setup: You are on a Teams call with Dr. Karen Liu, an orthopedic surgeon who controls the referral pathway. She opens with: We have seen three navigation pitches this quarter. Why should this one get committee time?
scenarios.objective: Earn a slot on the value analysis committee agenda with a designated clinical sponsor.

scenarios.label: Committee value review
scenarios.desc: A formal 45-minute committee session where clinicians, finance, IT, and supply chain interrogate ROI, cybersecurity, and workflow fit.
scenarios.setup: You are at the conference table with six stakeholders. The CFO opens with: Show us the cost-per-episode model with our actual payer mix, and the SOC-2 attestation.
scenarios.objective: Secure a conditional approval pending a 90-day pilot with predefined success metrics.

scenarios.label: Pilot terms negotiation
scenarios.desc: A follow-up negotiation with the OR director and materials manager to define pilot scope, data ownership, and conversion pricing.
scenarios.setup: You sit across from the OR director and materials manager. The director opens with: We will run the pilot, but our data stays here and the conversion price is capped at GPO minus 12 percent.
scenarios.objective: Finalize a pilot agreement with clear go/no-go criteria and a priced conversion path.
scenarios.moment: Monday 7:30 am, coffee on the table

buyers.angle: Prefers proven solutions with long track records for safety and compliance.
Needs clear cost-per-case savings and flexible financing options to justify spend.
Requires quantified ROI modeling and third-party validation before approval.
Eager to test new tools if they promise measurable patient outcome improvement.
Focuses on regulatory compliance and contract stability before exploring benefits.

objections: We need long-term evidence that this actually lowers infection rates
Our budget cycle doesn’t align with your proposal timeline
Why should we adopt this now when our current system works fine?
Can you show how this reduces cost per episode compared to our existing devices?
We require a formal cybersecurity audit report before any procurement committee will consider it
We need more concrete data on staff time savings before we can justify the investment
Our committee insists on seeing ROI projections tied to episode-based payment models
Flexible pricing sounds good, but we need proof it scales across multiple sites

rubric.label: Clinical evidence
rubric.what: Cites peer-reviewed outcomes and real-world registry data that match the committee’s patient population.

rubric.label: Economic modeling
rubric.what: Presents a cost-per-episode analysis using the facility’s actual payer mix, DRG weights, and variable cost inputs.

rubric.label: Stakeholder alignment
rubric.what: Addresses each committee role’s distinct concerns, clinical, financial, IT, supply chain, in their own language.

rubric.label: Compliance integrity
rubric.what: Accurately represents FDA clearance status, on-label indications, and adverse event reporting obligations without puffery.

rubric.label: Cybersecurity readiness
rubric.what: Provides SOC-2 Type II summaries, SBOM documentation, and a clear patch-management SLA for connected devices.

rubric.label: Pilot structuring
rubric.what: Defines measurable success criteria, data ownership, timeline, and a pre-negotiated conversion price before the pilot starts.

pitfalls: Promising off-label outcomes or implying superiority without head-to-head trial data.
Submitting a generic ROI calculator instead of a facility-specific cost-per-episode model.
Treating the clinical champion as the sole decision-maker and neglecting supply chain or IT requirements.
line: Selling medical devices to clinics and hospitals

research.text: Common objections from clinics and hospitals when selling medical devices include skepticism about effectiveness, timing issues, and lack of urgency. To address these, reps should offer flexible pricing plans, personalized demos, and ROI calculators. The shift to value-based care models has made clinical outcomes and cost-per-episode reductions crucial, and virtual selling is now essential. Committees demand quantified economic impact and cybersecurity attestations, and the buyer is often a committee rather than an individual.
